newsitem.title: USA: Dole declares campaign marathon to beat Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Dole declares campaign marathon to beat Clinton.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

Republican Bob Dole announced on Thursday he would campaign all day and all night for the last 96 hours of the U.S. presidential race in a herculean effort to prevent the re-election of President Bill Clinton.

Pushing his 73-year-old body to the limit, Dole vowed to hit the ground in at least 11 and possibly 15 states in a sleepless effort to round up votes that may set new standards for gruelling presidential campaign finales.
"The last time I fought round the clock for my country was in 1945 in Italy," Dole said, recalling his military service in World War II when he was seriously wounded.
"I will once again fight round-the-clock for America's future. Ninety-six hours of nonstop campaigning. From noon Friday until noon on Nov. 5," which is Election Day, he said.
"I am determined to make every hour of this decisive election count," he said at a rally in Miami. "The stakes are that high."

But the Dole campaign received a crushing blow from a new poll in California, which said Clinton had widened his lead from 10 to 18 points in the past two weeks -- even as Dole, in a costly and questionable strategy shift, threw himself into an effort to wrest the state away from Clinton.

He had decided to roll the dice in California after the earlier poll, figuring he could upset Clinton nationwide by stealing the state's 54 electoral votes, which are one-fifth of the 270 needed to win in the indirect U.S. system.

He poured $1.5 million a week into television spots and spent seven days in the state. In doing so, Dole pulled television advertising money out of other crucial states, virtually conceding them to Clinton.

"The campaign has crystallised. Clinton has a healthy double-digit lead and all signs are pointing to a fairly large Clinton win," said Mark Di Camillo of the Field Poll, which conducted the California survey.

The same could be said nationally, despite the fact that Dole narrowed Clinton's lead to 7.7 percentage points in the latest Reuters poll. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's support has been creeping towards the 10 percent mark.
A study of individual state polls by the Hotline political newsletter showed Clinton ahead in 35 states with 399 electoral votes. Dole led in 15 states with 135 votes.
Dole campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield said the 98-hour finale would be by bus, plane and other transport and would end in California.

Others have made extraordinary last-gasp efforts to reverse their fortunes in White House campaigns but few if any could match Dole's plan for non-stop activity over so long a time and so much territory.
Four years ago, Clinton campaigned nonstop for 30 hours from Philadelphia to Denver to his home base in Arkansas, but that was strictly by plane.
Clinton on Thursday focused on winning conservative-leaning Arizona, a feat no Democratic presidential candidate has managed since Harry Truman in 1948.
Revelling in his frontrunner status, the president also planned to criss-cross the country between now and next Tuesday making a final appeal for votes.
Speaking at a sun-drenched rally on the futuristic campus of Arizona State University, Clinton said the United States was "moving in the right direction."

"Compared to four years ago, we have 10 and a half million more jobs, we have the lowest combined rates of unemployment, inflation and home mortgage interest in 27 years," he said. "The deficit has been cut in all four years of my administration for the first time in the 20th century."
Clinton later flew on to conservative Nevada, another state normally hostile to Democratic presidential candidates, before ending the day in California.
Aides said he planned a major address on Friday on campaign finance reform.
